 Located just 2 hours from Atlanta and Nashville, Chattanooga is the USA’s first National Park City, and after exploring its outdoor adventures, incredible food scene, and historic railroad roots, it’s easy to see why.
 Here’s how to spend the perfect 4 days in Chattanooga and experience the best of what it has to offer👇🏼
 Day 1�🚂 Check into your vintage train car stay at Hotel Chalet�🍸 Enjoy dinner and drinks onsite at Elsie’s Daughter�🌅 Go for a whimsical sunset hike at Rock City

items.title: After years of service protecting the Chattanooga community, the Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is honoring the ret...
items.content_text:
After years of service protecting the Chattanooga community, the Chattanooga Police Department (CPD) is honoring the retirement of two members of its K9 Unit: K9 Burt, a decorated patrol and narcotics detection dog, and K9 Duke, who ultimately found his true calling outside of police work.
 K9 Burt, an 11-year-old Belgian Malinois, retired after 10 years of distinguished service with the CPD. As a narcotics detection canine, Burt was responsible for locating more than $3 million in illegal narcotics and currency during his career. Among his most significant contributions were three separate cases in which he located more than 1,000 fentanyl pills.
 “K9 Burt exemplified the courage and reliability that every handler hopes for in a partner,” said MPO Luke Timmons, Burt’s handler. “What makes me most proud is that no officers were ever injured by suspects during any of Burt’s deployments.”
 Having a single handler for an entire working career is a rarity among police K9s, making the partnership between Burt and Timmons even stronger. 
 Burt also earned recognition beyond Chattanooga for his exceptional performance in training and competition. He was named the United States Police Canine Association (USPCA) Regional Top Dog in both narcotics detection and dual-purpose certifications. During the USPCA Detector Dog Challenge, Burt earned first place honors in the room-search portion of the competition before an untimely bathroom break during the vehicle-search event derailed his chances at the overall title - even elite, highly trained police dogs go when they have to go.
 While K9 Duke’s career followed a different, less illustrious path, he will be remembered as part of the Chattanooga Police Department family.
 Despite many months of extensive training sessions, Duke consistently demonstrated that police work was not of interest to him. Ultimately, the K9 Unit retired Duke early and found him a loving home. Duke was originally purchased using grant funding, and all grant requirements were satisfied before his early retirement.
 The Chattanooga Police Department thanks both K9 Burt and K9 Duke for their time with the department and recognizes the commitment of the handlers, families, and community members who support the K9 Unit.
 The Chattanooga Police Department wishes both K9s a long, healthy retirement.

items.content_text:
Did you know our team has cleared of 40 downed trees since the beginning of May?
 Extreme weather conditions can weaken our trees, often leading to them coming down. When precipitation varies widely from extremely dry to extremely wet, this stresses out the tree. Dry conditions cause the tree to prioritize the usage of water often leading them to drop large branches, while wet conditions can weaken the tree's roots, causing the tree to fall altogether. No matter how healthy you may think your tree is, exposure to extreme weather conditions can damage the tree in a short amount of time. Always monitor your large trees for signs of degrading health. Check for things like soil cracking around the base of the tree, exposed roots, and prolonged “soupy” soil conditions. Call local arborists for professional advice on the health of your trees. 
 In the meantime, plant new trees! Don’t wait until you have one come down to plant another. Trees take years to grow and provide the shade that we admire them for. Late fall and winter are the best times to plant trees. This dormant period means the tree can invest all of its energy into its roots rather than diverting energy to leaf and fruit production. Check out the Chattanooga Tree Project to volunteer at tree plantings this winter and be on the lookout for free tree giveaways around the city.

💧🌿 What Has the Red Bank Stormwater Team Been Up To Recently? 🌿💧
 Last week, the Red Bank Public Works Stormwater Team was joined by local volunteers Don and Isabelle to continue restoration efforts along Stringers Branch near the Red Bank Police Department. Together, the team worked to remove invasive woody trees and treat invasive vines and low-growing vegetation with aquatic-safe herbicides. These invasive species were competing with and overtaking the native plants installed earlier this year during the Waterways Stream Restoration volunteer events.
 Native vegetation plays a critical role in maintaining healthy streams and waterways. Deep-rooted native plants help stabilize streambanks, reduce erosion, filter pollutants from stormwater runoff, provide habitat for local wildlife, and improve water quality before runoff enters our creeks and streams. Healthy streamside vegetation also helps absorb excess rainwater, reducing the impacts of flooding and protecting infrastructure downstream.
 Invasive species, on the other hand, can quickly dominate stream corridors, crowding out native plants, and reducing native biodiversity. Many invasive plants form dense monocultures that provide little value to wildlife and often have shallow root systems that are less effective at holding soil in place. As invasive species spread, they can contribute to increased erosion, degraded water quality, and the loss of important habitat for birds, pollinators, and other native wildlife.
 By removing invasive vegetation and encouraging the growth of native plants, the Stormwater Team and community volunteers are helping restore the natural health and function of Stringers Branch. These ongoing efforts will create a more resilient stream corridor that benefits both the environment and the residents of Red Bank for years to come.
 Want to help protect Red Bank's waterways? Consider planting native species in your landscape, learning about proper invasive species plant removal techniques, and joining future volunteer stream restoration events!
 We would also like to extend a special thank you to our partner, the Hamilton County Water Quality Department, for the Stream Buffer signs that they created. These help to ensure the area is protected from harmful vegetation removal in the future and explain the benefits of the stream restoration work that is ongoing here!
 #RedBankTN #RainSmart #NativePlants #StormwaterSmart #WaterQuality

Last week, the Red Bank Public Works Stormwater Team was joined by local volunteers Don and Isabelle to continue restoration efforts along Stringers Branch near the Red Bank Police Department. Together, the team worked to remove invasive woody trees and treat invasive vines and low-growing vegetation with aquatic-safe herbicides. These invasive species were competing with and overtaking the native plants installed earlier this year during the Waterways Stream Restoration volunteer events.
Native vegetation plays a critical role in maintaining healthy streams and waterways. Deep-rooted native plants help stabilize streambanks, reduce erosion, filter pollutants from stormwater runoff, provide habitat for local wildlife, and improve water quality before runoff enters our creeks and streams. Healthy streamside vegetation also helps absorb excess rainwater, reducing the impacts of flooding and protecting infrastructure downstream.
Invasive species, on the other hand, can quickly dominate stream corridors, crowding out native plants, and reducing native biodiversity. Many invasive plants form dense monocultures that provide little value to wildlife and often have shallow root systems that are less effective at holding soil in place. As invasive species spread, they can contribute to increased erosion, degraded water quality, and the loss of important habitat for birds, pollinators, and other native wildlife.
By removing invasive vegetation and encouraging the growth of native plants, the Stormwater Team and community volunteers are helping restore the natural health and function of Stringers Branch. These ongoing efforts will create a more resilient stream corridor that benefits both the environment and the residents of Red Bank for years to come.
Want to help protect Red Bank's waterways? Consider planting native species in your landscape, learning about proper invasive species plant removal techniques, and joining future volunteer stream restoration events!
We would also like to extend a special thank you to our partner, the Hamilton County Water Quality Department, for the Stream Buffer signs that they created. These help to ensure the area is protected from harmful vegetation removal in the future and explain the benefits of the stream restoration work that is ongoing here!

Last time I showed y'all where to eat in Chattanooga. Now let me show you what to do.
 We went to Raccoon Mountain Caverns, Ruby Falls, and Lookout Mountain, and yes, I know those are the most obvious things you can do in Chattanooga. They're obvious because they're GREAT. I went to Ruby Falls and Lookout Mountain as a kid and I'm happy to report the fairies and the whole Mother Goose world up there are still just as magical as I remembered.
 Now the caves. Both are beautiful and the lighting in each one will take your breath away, but they're two completely different experiences. Raccoon Mountain is smaller and more personal, and our guide Tristan taught me SO much about how caves form, the creatures that live down there, the whole cave biome, and how to protect it. Ruby Falls is the big tour, lots of people, and you go deep, deep underground to a watertall you won't believe, plus you learn the story of the people who found it. Do both. They're both worth it.
 Tell me: have you been? Did you get claustrophobic down in those caves? Did you love the fairies on Lookout Mountain as much as I did? And if you're from Chattanooga, what else should people be doing when they visit?

items.content_text:
TBI Investigating First In-Custody Death at Hamilton County Jail of 2026
 Hamilton County, TN – On the evening of August 10, 2026, Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office Corrections personnel were notified of an inmate experiencing a medical emergency.
 HCSO Corrections Deputies and contract medical personnel administered medical aid to the inmate identified as Colin Shannon, including administering Narcan and CPR while waiting on the arrival of EMS. Shannon was transported to a local hospital by Hamilton County Emergency Medical Service (HCEMS), where he was sadly pronounced deceased.
 The District Attorney was notified, and the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation (TBI) responded to conduct a full investigation. Once the investigation is complete, all findings will be turned over to the District Attorney's Office for review.
 Shannon was being housed at the jail for the following charges: 
 • Possession of Drug Paraphernalia 
 • Schedule II Drug Violations
 • Driving on Revoked, Suspended, or Cancelled License
 The HCSO asks that you keep Mr. Shannon's family and loved ones in your thoughts during this difficult time.
 This is the first in-custody death to occur at the Hamilton County Jail and Detention Center this year. This information is preliminary and subject to change. No further details are available.

Writers, check this out . . .
The Smithsonian Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage is partnering with the American Folklore Society to promote and document the festivals that comprise this year's "Of the People: The Smithsonian Festival of Festivals" initiative, a series of co-curated programs and exchanges showcasing the nation’s cultural landscape.
 We are seeking writers in the AFS community who can use their skills in ethnographic research, interviewing, and creative writing to help tell stories relating to the Of the People festivals, examining how communities remember, harmonize, move, and grow together through festive gatherings.
 Articles should be in the range of 1,600 to 2,500 words. Writing should be for a general audience. Writers are paid $500 for a completed article. Learn more: https://s.si.edu/4we2M72
 📸: Clarke Buehling treats guests to banjo tunes and stories on a historic streetcar ride at the inaugural Arkansas Folklife Festival. Photo by Sonya Pencheva, Ralph Rinzler Folklife Archives
 #2026Folklife #OfThePeople2026

 At a recent webinar looking ahead to the launch of #OECDPISA, #Youthwise member Nirajit Syamal spoke at the panel alongside with Andreas Schleicher, OECD Director for Education and Skills and Wendy Kopp, CEO and Co-founder of Teach For All. 
 In the lead-up to the launch of PISA, the world's largest survey of 15-year-old students, this webinar explored what measures of student success matter most while labour markets and technologies evolve. 
 The OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment compares how students perform in science, reading and maths, including computational problem-solving. 
 Ahead of #InternationalYouthDay, watch the webinar recap to explore why these data matter for preparing young people to navigate technological change and evolving labour markets: https://brnw.ch/21x4Qss 
 And save the date for the PISA launch: 
 📅 8 September | 09:30 CEST 
 #OECDyouth

 Step into the audience for Cue the Dice, Chattanooga Tabletop Revue's live-play Dungeons & Dragons series, where tabletop roleplaying becomes live theatre. Inspired by shows like Critical Role and Dimension 20, talented performers and community members gather around the stage to create an unforgettable story in real time—complete with dramatic roleplay, hilarious improvisation, unexpected twists, and the occasional catastrophic dice roll.

Whether you're a longtime D&D fan or have never played a tabletop game, this is a unique theatrical experience that's easy to follow and incredibly fun to watch.

items.content_text:
Sometimes the biggest takeaway from a day comes from the smallest moment.

Last week, members of our SETD team joined leaders from across the tri-state at Thrive Regional Partnership “Yes, And…” Summer Forum in South Pittsburg.

We toured the Lodge Cast Iron foundry and museum, saw firsthand the people and processes behind one of Southeast Tennessee’s most recognizable manufacturers, and joined conversations about transportation, infrastructure, community development, and what it takes to build a resilient future.

Along the way, one small moment stood out to us.

Inside the foundry, an employee has taken it upon himself to write a daily inspirational quote on a whiteboard for his coworkers. No one asked him to. He simply decided it was something he could do to encourage the people around him.

That day’s message: “A leader must inspire or his team will expire.”

It was a simple but meaningful reminder of something we see throughout our work at SETD: the strength of a region ultimately comes back to its people. The people who show up, share ideas, build things, collaborate, solve problems, encourage one another, and care about the communities they call home.

We’re grateful for Thrive Regional Partnership for creating opportunities like this.

Remember, if you suspect you're the victim of a scam, alert your bank to freeze your account, file a report with your local law enforcement, and report the scam to the FTC.

Estonia’s economy is recovering from a severe and prolonged recession.
 The recovery is expected to continue despite higher energy prices, with GDP growing by 1.8% this year and 2.7% in 2027. Nevertheless, uncertainty remains high due to potential risks from energy prices and geopolitical tensions.
 The country enjoys a robust business environment, a resilient labour market and a sound fiscal framework. But sustaining the recovery and ensuring fiscal sustainability requires continuing spending reviews, rethinking taxation, managing the energy transition and addressing climate change.
 Estonia is a digital frontrunner, but AI adoption remains uneven across the economy. Expanding uptake in traditional sectors and strengthening AI skills will be key to boost productivity and growth.
 Read the #OECD Economic Survey of Estonia: https://brnw.ch/21x4O8H
 #BetterPoliciesForBetterLives

How can public and private actors work together to strengthen economic resilience in an increasingly uncertain world?
 Geopolitical tensions worldwide are rising, including active conflicts in the Middle East and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
 These conflicts have shown how quickly war can disrupt trade, investment and livelihoods.
 Physical damage, blocked transport routes, contract disruption and asset seizures often fall outside standard insurance coverage, precisely when protection is most needed.

 Join us August 22–29 at Fort Monroe as we remember the arrival of the first recorded Africans in English North America in 1619, honor their lives and legacy, celebrate the cultures and traditions carried forward through generations, and reflect on a story that continues to shape our nation.
 Throughout the week, experience commemorative ceremonies, music, dance, drumming, conversations, family programs and special events that invite people of all ages to learn, reflect and participate.
 The week culminates on Saturday, August 29, with the unveiling of the newest sculpture at the African Landing Memorial—continuing the story of the men, women and children whose lives are connected to this historic place.

HONORING THE SACRIFICE
 The  American Heroes Dinner last night focused on life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness ￼ and the decisions we make based on the circumstances of our life. 🇺🇸🇺🇸
 ￼Andrew and Judge Tori Smith and their family do an amazing with the Foundation helping veterans and their families across the country with assistance and encouragement while recognizing great American wounded Patriots!
 Keynote speaker Navy Seal Jason Redman, USN (Ret) served 15 years was ambushed in￼ Iraq during a mission to capture Al Quada operatives, resulting in his traumatic injuries. Thirty-seven surgeries and almost twenty years later, Redman’s story compels listeners to choose service to others and with tenacity and perseverance. 
 Special guests tonight at my  table included Ooltewah High School Basketball Coach  Tony Williams and players, Jeremiah Wells and Elijah Wiley. ￼Also patriot Matt Hilliard and  wife Erica Miller Hilliard.
 God bless  our wounded warriors and their families!
 ￼ 
 State Representative Greg Vital

UTC LIVE! will move most of its 2026-27 performances to Cadek Hall, giving the series a smaller setting that better fits the artists and programs it presents.
 Known for bringing noted artists to campus who are outside the mainstream, UTC LIVE! will present jazz, Danish folk music, a historically informed Beethoven program and a marimba recital, with most of the season taking place in Cadek Hall’s 217-seat recital hall—a space especially well suited for piano, jazz and other acoustic performances. The smaller setting also brings audiences closer to the stage, allowing eye contact between performers and audience members.
 🔗  Read more here: https://blog.utc.edu/…/utc-live-announces-2026-27-season-w…/
